sessions.title: Carried, Not Shamed
sessions.aim: To recover the church as the place where the crushed are carried rather than hidden, to name the shame and secrecy that have made congregations unsafe for people who are suffering, and to call a community to bear one another's burdens the way four friends carried a paralyzed man to Jesus through a roof.
sessions.summary:
Many people sit in the same pew for years and sink into a depression no one sees, until the loneliest place they've ever been is the middle of a church that thinks they're fine. That failure is ours.

What is the church for people who are suffering inside it? Scripture is plain. "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). "Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed" (James 5:16). "If one member suffers, all suffer together" (1 Corinthians 12:26). And in Mark 2 four friends tear open a roof to lower a paralyzed man to Jesus, and Jesus sees "their faith."

Some will say private struggles should stay private and church is for worship and teaching, not group therapy. There's a real caution there against turning the church into nothing but a support group. But it can't stand against the plain command to carry each other, and it often hides a preference for a church that costs us nothing. We built a culture where everyone performs being fine, and the shame that keeps the depressed silent in the pew is more ours than theirs. The church is meant to be the one place on earth you can stop pretending and be carried when you can't walk. We can repent and become that again.

keyScripture.why: "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). Carrying each other's weight isn't an optional kindness. It's how Christ's law is fulfilled, and it's the plainest answer to a church that leaves its suffering people to carry their load alone.

discussion.q: For many who suffer, the loneliest place they've been is the middle of a church that thinks they're fine. Where have you performed being fine at church while carrying something heavy, or watched someone else do it?
discussion.behind: Open gently, but don't skip it, because nearly everyone in the room has done this. You're bringing out the gap between the smiling surface of church life and the real weights people carry into the building and take back out unshared. Let the room feel how common the performance is, and begin to call it a loss rather than a virtue.

discussion.q: Read Galatians 6:2 and James 5:16. What makes it so hard to actually do this at church? What would have to change for it to be safe?
discussion.behind: Let people name the barriers plainly. Many don't confess because they've seen what happens to those who do: the gossip, the awkwardness, the quiet demotion. Help the room name what makes their church unsafe, not to condemn anyone but to see clearly what would have to change. The command is plain, so the question is what's blocking obedience to it.

discussion.q: Read Mark 2:1-12. Four friends tear open a roof, and Jesus sees "their faith" (Mark 2:5). What does it mean that sometimes you have to be carried by someone else's faith when you have none of your own?
discussion.behind: Let the picture do its work, because it's freeing. The paralyzed man brought nothing but his need, and Jesus honored the friends' faith. For the person too depressed to believe or pray, this says the community can carry them to Christ when they can't get there themselves. Help the room see both roles: the one who has to let himself be carried, and the friends willing to dig through a roof.

discussion.q: Some say private struggles should stay private and church is for worship, not group therapy. What's true in that, and where does it become an excuse for a church that leaves its wounded alone?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. There's a real caution against shrinking the church into a circle where nothing is left but everyone's problems, and not every struggle belongs in front of the whole congregation. Honor that. But the caution often hides something less noble, a preference for a tidy church over a costly one, and it can't stand against the command to bear each other's burdens. Help the room tell wise discretion from the self-protective distance that abandons people.

discussion.q: How have you helped make honesty costly at church? What would turning from that look like in this room?
discussion.behind: This isn't about blaming a vague "them." It's each person, the leader first, owning how they've made honesty expensive: by gossip, by recoiling from weakness, by rewarding the performance of being fine. Then turn toward hope: a room can decide to be different. End by making this group a concrete first instance of the carrying it describes, and make sure everyone knows that real crises need real help, including 988, alongside the community's care.

objections.objection: People should keep their private struggles private and not dump their problems on the church. A congregation is for worship and teaching and the word of God, not for turning every gathering into group therapy.
objections.response: There's a real caution here worth keeping. A church is more than a support group. Its center is the worship of God and the preaching of his word, and there's a way of making everything about our problems that shrinks a congregation into endless processing with God nowhere in the middle. Not every struggle belongs in front of everyone, and discretion is wisdom, not avoidance. But the objection can't stand against the direct commands: bear one another's burdens, confess to one another, weep with those who weep, when one suffers all suffer. And it often hides a less admirable motive than it admits. What calls itself a preference for privacy is often a preference for comfort, for a tidy church that costs us nothing and never asks us to enter anyone's real pain. The early church carried its weak, its widows, and its sick, and that carrying wasn't a distraction from worship. It was the law of Christ being fulfilled. A church that preaches a God who bears our burdens and won't bear its own members' burdens has contradicted its own sermon.

objections.objection: If I share what I'm really going through, it'll just turn into gossip, or people will treat me differently, or they'll try to fix me with a verse and a quick answer. It's safer to keep it to myself.
objections.response: This isn't really an objection to the command. It's testimony that the church has failed the command, and it needs to be heard as the wound it is, not argued down. You're right that many churches aren't safe. Confession has too often become fuel for gossip, and vulnerable people have been sidelined or managed or handed a verse instead of being held. That fault is the church's, not yours. But the church's failure doesn't cancel the calling. It calls us to repent and become what we're supposed to be. And notice the cost of protecting yourself. Keeping it all to yourself, safe as it feels, is exactly how a person ends up alone in the middle of a church that thinks they're fine. The answer isn't to trust everyone, which would be foolish. It's to find the safe few, the friends who will carry instead of gossip, and let them lower you through the roof. And it's on the rest of us to build a church where that trust isn't a gamble. James ties healing to confessing to one another. Hidden, a wound festers. Carried, it can begin to close.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who are the two or three people who could be your roof-tearing friends, the ones who'd carry you to Christ when you can't get there yourself? What's keeping you from letting them?
sessions.practice: This week, do two things. First, stop performing fine with at least one safe person. Tell them what you're actually carrying, and let yourself, for once, be the one lowered through the roof instead of the one who's always fine. Second, be a roof-tearer for someone else. Notice the person at church who's performing fine, move toward them, and carry part of their weight without waiting to be asked. Write down what it cost you to tell the truth, and what it cost you to move toward someone else's pain, because both are the law of Christ. And if the person you move toward is in danger, do not carry that alone either, get them real help and, if their life is at risk, 988.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've built churches where a person can sit for years in the middle of your people and call it the loneliest place they've known, and the shame that kept them silent was more ours than theirs. Forgive us for performing fine, for recoiling from weakness, for using your word to end a conversation instead of entering a life. Make us a people who bear one another's burdens, who confess and aren't betrayed, who weep with those who weep, who tear open roofs to carry our friends to you when they can't walk. For anyone in this room hiding a great weight behind a smile, give them a safe few, and make us those few. Teach us that carrying one another is no distraction from worship but its truest form. And where anyone is in real danger, make us people who don't look away but reach out, get help, and stay. Amen.
reflection: Where have I performed being fine at church while carrying something real? What taught me that hiding was safer than telling the truth?
Have I helped make honesty costly, by gossip or recoil or the quick answer? What would turning from that look like the next time someone is open with me?
Who could carry me to Christ when I can't get there myself? And whom is God asking me to carry?
sessions.teaching:
Think of a man who sits in the same pew of the same church for years. He's a familiar face, always polite, always fine, and he sinks slowly into a depression that not one person in that congregation ever sees. For a man like that, the loneliest place on earth is the middle of a church that thinks he's fine. That's a failure, and it isn't his. It's ours.

So the last question of this study is what the church is for people who are suffering inside it. Is it a place that carries the crushed, or a place they quietly learn to hide from? Scripture isn't subtle about this. "Bear one another's burdens," Paul tells the Galatians, "and so fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). That's a startling thing to say: carrying each other's weight isn't a nice extra in the Christian life but the very fulfillment of Christ's law. "Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed," James writes (James 5:16), tying healing to honesty, so that what stays hidden stays sick. "If one member suffers, all suffer together," Paul tells the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 12:26), because the body is one and can't wall off the pain of one part.

The picture that gathers it all up is in Mark 2. Four friends carry a paralyzed man to Jesus and can't get through the crowd. So they climb up, dig through the roof, and lower him on his mat right in front of the Lord. And Mark says, "when Jesus saw their faith" (Mark 2:5), he spoke to the man, forgave his sins, and then told him to get up and walk. Their faith. The man on the mat brought nothing but his need. It was his friends who believed enough to tear open a roof, and Jesus honored it.

The other side should be heard, because sincere people hold it. Private struggles should stay private, they'd say. People shouldn't dump their problems on the congregation. The church exists for worship and the word, not to turn every gathering into group therapy. There's a real caution in that I want to keep. A church can lose its center and become nothing but a circle of endless processing with God nowhere in the middle. Not every struggle belongs in front of everyone, and discretion is wisdom, not cowardice.

But that view can't survive the plain commands to carry each other. And if I'm truthful about myself and about most of us, the preference for keeping things private usually hides a preference for keeping things comfortable. We don't really want a church where people tell the truth about what they're carrying, because truth is inconvenient. It asks something of us. It interrupts the tidy service and the pleasant coffee hour with someone's real pain. So without ever deciding to, we built a culture of performed wellness. The expected answer to "How are you?" is "Good." Weakness is a quiet liability. People who are suffering learn fast to read the room and act fine.

That means the shame that keeps the man in the pew silent isn't mainly his. It's ours. We made the room he's ashamed in. By a thousand small signals we taught him that his real self wasn't welcome and that the price of belonging was a smile and a lie. Most of us have helped build that, pastors and members alike: recoiling from the person whose pain was too much, reaching for a verse to close a conversation we didn't want to enter, rewarding the people who seemed fine and finding the open ones exhausting. We did this. And because we did it, we can repent of it.

The church is meant to be the one place on earth where you can finally stop pretending, where you can be carried when you can't walk, lowered through the roof by friends when you have no strength and no faith of your own, and not be shamed for needing it. That isn't a distraction from the church's real work. It is the church's real work, the people of a God who bore our burdens learning to bear each other's. We stopped being that place. We can become it again, and it starts small, in rooms like this one, when a few people decide to stop performing and start carrying. And when the weight you find in another is more than a friend can carry, when there is real danger, do not carry it alone or in secret, get them to real help, and if a life is at risk, call or text 988, because sometimes bearing a burden means refusing to let someone bear it in the dark by themselves. The man in the pew should never have been that alone. In the body of Christ, no one has to be.

scriptureStudy.note: "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ." Carrying each other is named as the fulfillment of Christ's own law. A church that leaves its suffering to carry their load alone has failed the law it preaches.

"Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed." Healing is tied to honesty spoken in community. The shame that keeps struggles hidden also keeps them from the confession that begins to heal them.
"If one member suffers, all suffer together." The body can't treat the pain of one part as nobody else's concern. A member's suffering belongs to the whole body by design.

"Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep." The command to weep with the weeping rules out the rush to fix or to cheer. It asks for the harder gift of entering someone's grief and staying there.

"And when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay. And when Jesus saw their faith..." Four friends dig through a roof for a man who can't come himself, and Jesus honors their faith. A community can carry the one who has no strength left.

"For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!" Scripture names the danger of isolation plainly. It's the danger every hidden sufferer lives in.

"The God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction." Comfort received in suffering is given so it can be handed on. Those who were carried become carriers.

sessions.goingDeeper:
A group that wants to go further can look at what has happened to community in general, because the church's failure to carry its suffering didn't happen in a vacuum. Sociologists such as Robert Putnam, in Bowling Alone (2000), documented a long decline in the clubs, congregations, and close ties that used to hold Americans together. The loneliness the man in the pew felt is partly the church taking on a loneliness the whole culture now runs on. In 2023 the U.S. Surgeon General issued an advisory calling loneliness and isolation a public health concern and comparing their effect on early death to smoking up to fifteen cigarettes a day.

That finding confirms what Scripture said from the start: "It is not good that the man should be alone" (Genesis 2:18). But bring the finding under Scripture, not just beside it. Research can measure the damage of isolation. It can't supply the cure, which isn't simply more social contact but a particular kind of community, the body of Christ, bound together not by shared tastes or convenience but by a shared Lord who carried our burdens first.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote Life Together in 1938, after leading an underground seminary the Nazi government had shut down. In it he argued, in substance, that a pious fellowship which lets no one be a sinner leaves everyone hiding their sin, and so leaves no one able to find help (paraphrased). Then ask the hardest question. If the church is meant to be where the burdened are carried, its failure to be that is a betrayal of what it is. What would real repentance look like for us: not a program, but a change in how we meet the truth when someone finally tells it?
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is well liked and always upbeat. He asks after everyone else and deflects every question about himself with a joke, and over several weeks you start to sense that the steady cheer is a wall. Then, after a session on being carried, he stays behind and tells you, haltingly, that he's been in a very dark place for a long time. He's never told anyone at church, because he didn't want to be a burden or lose the role he plays for everyone.

How you respond will show whether the group's talk about carrying was real. Don't react with alarm, and don't turn him into a project. Either would confirm his fear that his real self isn't welcome. Receive what he told you as the trust it is. Tell him plainly he isn't a burden, and that carrying him isn't a favor but the law of Christ, the very thing you've all been talking about.

Then move gently but concretely, because vague sympathy is its own kind of abandonment, help him take a real step toward help, a counselor, a doctor, whatever his situation needs, and if there is any sign of danger, act on it at once and make sure he knows about 988. Don't let him slip back into the role of the one who's always fine. And consider, with his permission, whether letting the group carry him a little might free others who are still hiding. The point isn't to expose him. It's to make sure that this time, the man who told the truth is met with carrying and not with the awkward distance that taught him to hide.

memoryVerse.text: Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.

leaderPrimer:
A study on mental health can drift, without anyone meaning it to, into one of two ditches. In the first, the group becomes an amateur clinic, and kind people start diagnosing each other and giving advice they aren't qualified to give. In the second, the group makes everything spiritual, and someone's real illness gets treated as a faith problem to be prayed away, which is exactly the cruelty this study exists to bury. Steer between them. You aren't a therapist and this isn't therapy, and you should say so the first night. You're a group of people learning to tell God the truth and to carry one another, and where someone needs real help, your job isn't to be that help but to make sure they get it.

Know your resources before you begin. Have the number of a trusted Christian counselor, know how your church refers people to care, and keep this in front of you at all times, that in the United States the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is reached by calling or texting 988, any hour of any day. If anyone in your group discloses that they are thinking of ending their life, that is not a discussion topic, it is an emergency, and you respond to it as one, staying with them, connecting them to 988 or emergency services, and not leaving them alone.

Set the culture from the first session. What's said here stays here. No one gets diagnosed, fixed, or handed a verse to end a hard moment. Some of the most important things will be said quietly, or afterward, or not at all, so make room for that rather than asking for confession across the circle. And watch for the person who is performing fine, the one whose cheerful deflection is a wall, because that's often the person carrying the most.

Don't lead this from above. If you present yourself as the one who has it together while everyone else struggles, the room will perform right back at you and no one will tell the truth. Go in as a fellow sufferer who has found, in the dark, a God who holds on when you can't. Five weeks won't cure anyone's depression or anxiety, and you shouldn't pretend they will. But they can make one room on earth a place where a suffering person doesn't have to hide, where the weight gets shared instead of performed, and where the path to real help always stays in view.

faq.q: Is this study going to tell people that their depression or anxiety is a sin or a lack of faith?
faq.a: No. It works hard against that lie. It points to Elijah asking to die, David whose tears were his food, Jeremiah cursing the day of his birth, Job whom God calls blameless sitting in ashes, Paul who despaired of life itself, and Jesus sorrowful to the point of death. If the dark fell on all of them, it isn't simple evidence of spiritual failure. The study does make room for the truth that some heaviness comes from sin and lifts when it's confessed. But it refuses to read illness as a moral judgment. Where the darkness is an illness, the study calls for care, not accusation, and it treats therapy, medication, and a doctor's help as gifts of God. No one in this study is told to just believe harder.

faq.q: What if someone in the group is thinking about ending their life?
faq.a: Take it with complete seriousness. It's a real possibility in any group, and the study is built to make room for it rather than look away. If anyone tells you they're thinking of ending their life, it isn't a discussion topic. It's an emergency. Stay with them, don't leave them alone, and connect them right away to real help. In the United States the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is reached by calling or texting 988, available every hour of every day, and if there is immediate danger, contact emergency services. The leader primer asks you to know your resources before the study begins, including a trusted counselor and your church's way of referring people to care. Believe the person, don't minimize what they've said, don't try to be their therapist, and get them to help that's equipped for it. Staying alive long enough to be helped is itself an act of courage and faith, and the study says so.

faq.q: Does the study actually support therapy and medication, or is it going to be suspicious of them like some churches are?
faq.a: It supports them plainly, and session 2 is given over to taking apart the false choice between faith and treatment. It points to Luke "the beloved physician" traveling with Paul, to Paul's remedy for Timothy's stomach, to the Samaritan pouring oil and wine on wounds, and to Jesus saying it's the sick who need a doctor. It argues that the brain is an organ that gets sick like any other. The doctor, the counselor, and the medicine aren't competitors with God's grace but ways it comes, what theologians call common grace. Refusing help in the name of faith often turns out to be pride or fear dressed up as devotion, and the study names the harm done when suffering people are shamed away from care. In this study, getting treatment is a yes to the God who provided it.

faq.q: Isn't it dangerous for a small group with no training to talk about serious mental health?
faq.a: It would be dangerous to pretend the group is something it isn't, and the study is careful never to do that. It says plainly that the group isn't a clinic and the leader isn't a therapist, and that where someone needs real help, the group's job is to make sure they get it. Leaders are asked to know their resources before beginning, to keep the crisis line in view, and to treat any sign of danger as an emergency for professionals, not for the group. Within those limits an untrained group can do something valuable and safe: tell God the truth, carry one another, and keep the way to real help visible. The danger isn't in talking openly about suffering. It's in a church where nobody talks about it at all.

faq.q: Why does the study spend a whole session just on how the Bible speaks about anguish?
faq.a: Because the most common lie suffering Christians carry is that their darkness is unspiritual, an insult to a book of joy, something to hide from God. Session 1 takes that lie apart by showing how crowded Scripture is with faithful people in the dark, and how God meets them with bread and rest and a whisper instead of a rebuke. God even kept Psalm 88, a prayer that ends in darkness, in his people's songbook. Until a suffering person knows their darkness is welcome before God, nothing else in the study can land, because they'll keep hiding the very thing they most need to bring.

faq.q: What's the difference between depression as an illness and heaviness that comes from sin?
faq.a: The study holds both without folding one into the other. Some heaviness of soul does come from real sin, and that kind lifts when the sin is brought into the light and confessed. But much depression comes down on obedient, prayerful people with no cause they can find, the way a fever comes, a real illness of brain and body that's no more a moral failure than a failing kidney. One way to tell them apart: the Spirit's conviction is specific and leads toward grace, while depression's accusation is vague and total and leads only to despair. When the darkness is an illness, the study calls for care, not confession, and warns against doing what Job's friends did, adding false accusation to suffering. When in doubt, care for the person and keep the path to help open.

faq.q: Isn't telling anxious people to bring their fear to God just a religious version of positive thinking?
faq.a: No. Positive thinking tells you to produce calm by willpower, which only heaps shame on anxious people when they can't. Philippians 4 doesn't command a feeling. It gives the fear somewhere to go, into God's hands through specific prayer, and promises a peace "which surpasses all understanding," which by definition isn't something you engineer. The study also takes seriously that anxiety lives in the body, and that bodily anxiety may need bodily help, including a doctor's care, alongside prayer. The peace it offers isn't a technique you master but a gift that guards you in the storm. Positive thinking asks you to make the feeling yourself. This is the opposite.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I've struggled with my own mental health, or still do?
faq.a: That doesn't disqualify you. It may be what qualifies you. The study was written for ordinary people, not clinicians: every discussion question has a note behind it, every objection has a response, and every session ends in prayer. A leader who performs having it all together teaches the room to perform right back, and then no one tells the truth. Your own struggle, named at the right moments, can make the room safe for everyone else's. You don't need to have arrived. You need to be willing to be truthful, to keep the room safe, and to know where real help is. Read the leader primer, settle your own heart, know your resources including the 988 crisis line, and lead as a fellow traveler in the dark who has found a God who holds on.

faq.q: Why does the study talk about the church's failures instead of just helping the person who is suffering?
faq.a: Because a lot of the suffering it addresses was made worse by the church. Many pulpits have treated illness as weak faith, and many congregations have built a culture of performed wellness where hurting people learn to hide. You can't help someone while blaming them for wounds the community helped cause, and you can't repent of something you still call a virtue. Owning the church's share isn't a distraction from helping the sufferer. It's part of helping them, because it's what turns a room into a place where people are carried instead of accused.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic, and this sounds like religion telling depressed people their problems are spiritual. Is that what this is?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and the study answers it by refusing that move. It doesn't tell depressed people their problems are merely spiritual. It says the brain is an organ that gets sick like any other, that therapy and medication are real goods to receive without shame, and that treating illness as weak faith is cruel. What it offers instead isn't a diagnosis but company: the claim that the God of the Bible isn't found shouting instructions from a safe distance but inside the darkness, and that Jesus himself cried out "forsaken." You don't have to share that belief to notice that a faith which keeps a prayer with no happy ending in its book, and insists the suffering be carried rather than shamed, is different from the religion you may have met. The study only asks you to see it clearly.

faq.q: Does taking faith seriously mean the study looks down on people who rely mainly on medication and therapy to cope?
faq.a: No. The study treats medication and therapy as gifts of God and never ranks them below prayer or treats leaning on them as a lesser path. It does offer something it believes medicine and therapy can't finally supply, a hope grounded in a God who is present in the dark and holds on when the sufferer can't. But it offers that as a gift, not a rebuke. The person doing well because of their medication and their counselor is, in this study, receiving God's provision, not settling for a substitute. Every good means of healing, medical and spiritual, comes from the same God, so a sufferer can receive all of it without shame.

faq.q: What if the study stirs up something heavy in me or someone else that we aren't ready to handle?
faq.a: That's a real possibility, and it's better to name it than fear it. Talking openly about suffering can bring up what's been buried. Often that's good, because what stays hidden stays sick. But it also means the group needs somewhere to send what it can't hold. This is exactly why the leader primer insists that leaders know their resources before beginning, a trusted counselor, the church's referral process, and the 988 crisis line for anyone in danger. If the study stirs something up in you, it doesn't mean something went wrong. It means it touched something real. Don't push it back down. Bring it to a safe person and, if you need to, a professional. The group's job isn't to resolve everything that surfaces but to make sure no one carries it alone or in secret.

timeline.event: In the reign of King Ahab, the prophet Elijah flees into the wilderness after Mount Carmel, sits under a broom tree, and asks God to take his life. God answers with bread, sleep, and a low whisper (1 Kings 19).
David's psalms of lament, in which tears are his food and God feels far away, are kept in Israel's songbook rather than edited out, and lament becomes a lasting language of faith.
Jeremiah, in the middle of his calling, curses the day of his birth and asks why he was born to see toil and sorrow (Jeremiah 20:14-18). God doesn't remove him from his work.
In Gethsemane Jesus says his soul is "very sorrowful, even to death," and on the cross he cries out, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" The sinless Son enters the felt darkness himself.

Paul writes to the Corinthians that he was burdened beyond his strength and "despaired of life itself." In another letter he sends greetings from "Luke the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14), a doctor among his closest companions.
Basil of Caesarea builds a large house of care for the sick and the poor outside Caesarea, often counted among the first Christian hospitals. Care for bodies and care for souls belong together.
The Spanish friar John of the Cross writes his poem and commentary on the dark night of the soul, giving the church language for a spiritual darkness that is not sin.
Robert Burton, an English clergyman, publishes The Anatomy of Melancholy, a long and sympathetic study that treats deep sadness as a condition to understand and care for, not only to condemn.
Charles Spurgeon publishes the first series of Lectures to My Students, including "The Minister's Fainting Fits," where he writes openly about his own recurring depression.

The first edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders is published. The decades that follow bring modern psychiatric medicine, relief earlier generations could only endure without.

The United States consolidates its crisis services under the three-digit number 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, making immediate help reachable by call or text at any hour, a modern instrument of the mercy Scripture always commanded toward the desperate.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here. It takes courage to sit in a room and talk about the weight we carry. Before we start, a few things. First, this isn't a clinic and I'm not a therapist. None of us is here to diagnose or fix anyone. We're here to tell God the truth and learn to carry one another. Second, what's said here stays here. Nobody will be handed a verse to end a hard moment, and nobody will be treated differently for being truthful. Third, I'm not up here as someone who has it all figured out. Some of us are in this right now, and that's welcome. One more thing, and it matters more than the rest. If any of you is in danger, if you are thinking about ending your life, that is not something to hide or handle alone, and you can come to me privately, and there is help available every hour of every day by calling or texting 988. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. I'll read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone says anything. There are no wrong answers in the first few minutes.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what this passage says. Now let's bring it home, out of the ideas and into the actual weight each of us walked in here carrying, because none of this matters if it stays a discussion about suffering in general.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though it isn't resolved. A weight like this doesn't lift in an evening, and I'm not going to tie a bow on it. Take what got stirred up home with you instead of pushing it back down. Try the practice this week, gently, and sit with the reflection questions on your own. If something heavy surfaced tonight, do not carry it alone, tell a safe person, and if you are in any danger, reach for help right away, including 988. Come back ready to be truthful, not finished. Let me pray for us before we go. My door is open, and you don't have to be fine to walk through it.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety, confidentiality, and not diagnosing one another, and make sure everyone knows the group is not a substitute for real help, including 988.
Week 2: Session 1, The Honesty of the Broom Tree, with extra time in the lament psalms.
Week 3: Session 2, The False Choice Between Faith and Help, part one: Luke, the Samaritan, and the brain as an organ.
Week 4: Session 2 continued: the objections about medication and testing God, with room for people's own experiences of treatment.
Week 5: Session 3, Anxiety, the Body, and the Peace That Is Not a Formula.
Week 6: Session 4, The Dark Night That Is Not Sin. Take care for anyone in the dark and keep the crisis resources visible.
Week 8: Bringing it together. Look back over the five practices and the Scripture index, talk about what each person is carrying home, and close with Psalm 34:18.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together: how the Bible speaks about anguish, and the false choice between faith and help.
Week 2: Session 3, Anxiety, the Body, and the Peace That Is Not a Formula.
Week 3: Session 4, The Dark Night That Is Not Sin. Name the crisis resources plainly and take care for the room.
Week 4: Session 5, Carried, Not Shamed, with a short closing time on the God who holds on in the dark.

bibliography.title: Spurgeon's Sorrows: Realistic Hope for Those Who Suffer from Depression
bibliography.author: Zack Eswine
bibliography.note: A pastor's short book on Charles Spurgeon's lifelong depression and how he preached through it. Darkness can fall on the most faithful. Supports sessions 1 and 4.

bibliography.title: Grace for the Afflicted: A Clinical and Biblical Perspective on Mental Illness
bibliography.author: Matthew S. Stanford
bibliography.note: A Christian neuroscientist treats mental illness as real illness and holds the biblical and the clinical together. Supports session 2.

bibliography.title: Dark Clouds, Deep Mercy: Discovering the Grace of Lament
bibliography.author: Mark Vroegop
bibliography.note: A pastor recovers the biblical language of lament, its shape and its place in the life of faith. Supports sessions 1 and 4.

bibliography.title: The Dark Night of the Soul
bibliography.author: John of the Cross
bibliography.note: The sixteenth-century classic on a spiritual darkness that purifies rather than punishes. Background for session 4. Read it with care, and never use it to treat a medical illness as a spiritual stage.

bibliography.title: A Grief Observed
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis's journal of his grief after his wife's death and the felt absence of God within it, a faith that keeps speaking to God from the dark. Background for sessions 1 and 4.

bibliography.title: Life Together
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: A short book on Christian community written in 1938 after the underground seminary he led was closed. Its chapter on confession argues that a fellowship where no one may admit sin leaves everyone alone with it. Supports session 5.

bibliography.title: The Anatomy of Melancholy
bibliography.author: Robert Burton
bibliography.note: The seventeenth-century clergyman's long, sympathetic study of melancholy, an early example of treating deep sadness as a condition to understand rather than only condemn. Historical background.

bibliography.title: Local counseling and crisis care
bibliography.author: Your church and community
bibliography.note: Not a single book but a category. Leaders should identify trusted local counselors, their church's referral process, and the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline before beginning, and keep these ready throughout the study.

bibliography.title: The Psalms of lament, read straight through
bibliography.author: The psalmists
bibliography.note: The main biblical text for the whole study, especially Psalms 13, 42, 43, and 88, where God's people speak to him from the dark. To be read and prayed, not only cited.

bibliography.title: The book of Job
bibliography.author: Unknown
bibliography.note: A blameless man in the depths whose comforters wound him with false explanations. Central to the study's refusal to read suffering as a sentence passed on the sufferer. Read it for both Job's darkness and the friends' mistake.

furtherReading: Spurgeon's Sorrows, Zack Eswine, for anyone who wants a faithful pastor's company in the dark of depression. Behind sessions 1 and 4.
Grace for the Afflicted, Matthew S. Stanford, for readers who want the clinical and biblical picture of mental illness held together. Behind session 2.
Dark Clouds, Deep Mercy, Mark Vroegop, for anyone who wants to relearn the language of lament behind session 1.
Life Together, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for anyone wrestling with why confessing to one another is so hard and so freeing. Behind session 5.
The Psalms of lament, especially 13, 42, and 88, read and prayed straight through, for anyone willing to let Scripture give them words for the dark.

glossary.definition: The Bible's language of complaint, grief, and even accusation spoken directly to God, found in about a third of the Psalms. It isn't a failure of faith but one of its forms: faith speaking from the floor instead of going silent.

The place in 1 Kings 19 where Elijah, days after his greatest victory, asks God to let him die and is met with bread, sleep, and a whisper. In this study, shorthand for God's tenderness toward the despairing.

The good God gives through human hands and knowledge, including the skill of doctors and counselors and the chemistry of medicine, even through people who don't know him. It's why treatment is a gift of God, not a rival to him.

glossary.term: The dark night of the soul
glossary.definition: John of the Cross's name for a season when God feels absent while he does his deepest hidden work, a darkness that purifies rather than punishes. It isn't the same as clinical depression, though the two can overlap, and it's never a reason to deny anyone medical care.

The idea, forced on many suffering people, that they must choose between faith and treatment, or trust and medication, as if the two were rivals. Scripture doesn't make that choice, and neither does this study.

A real illness of brain and body that can come on faithful people without cause and without fault, no more a moral failure than a fever. To be met with care and with the comfort of a God near to the brokenhearted, never with the charge of weak faith.

Fear suffered largely in the body, a nervous system stuck in an alarm it was built to sound only briefly. It isn't a simple choice that can be commanded away. Philippians 4 meets it not with a formula for calm but with prayer and a peace that guards the heart.

The peace of God in Philippians 4:7. Paul's word for "guard" is a military one, like soldiers posted around a city. The peace stands watch over the heart in the middle of fear rather than removing it. It's a gift, not a calm we produce by trying harder.

The picture in Deuteronomy 33:27 of God's support beneath the lowest place the darkness can drag a person. It grounds a hope that doesn't depend on being felt, because what holds the sufferer is God's grip and not their own.

A church culture where people learn to answer "good" to every question and hide what they carry, which makes the congregation unsafe for the truth. This study names it as something the community built and needs to repent of.

From the four friends in Mark 2 who dug through a roof to lower their paralyzed friend to Jesus. Shorthand for a community that carries the one who has no strength or faith of their own, and whose faith Jesus honors.

The three-digit number for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the United States, reached by call or text at any hour. Kept visible throughout the study as the path to immediate help for anyone in danger, alongside the community's ordinary care.

quoteCards: Faith doesn't mean never falling. Very often it's what keeps talking to God from the floor.
Heaven's answer to a prophet who wanted to die wasn't a lecture on gratitude. It was bread, and sleep, and a whisper.
The brain is an organ. It gets sick like any other. We just make a moral issue of it in a way we never would with the heart.
The doctor, the counselor, and the medicine aren't competitors with grace. They're among the ways it comes.
God didn't promise the storm would stop. He promised a peace that would guard you while it rages.
Depression can take away the sense of God long before it could ever take away the fact of him.
You don't hold on to God in the dark. He holds on to you.
For many who suffer, the loneliest place on earth is the middle of a church that thinks they're fine.
